article_title: Efficacy of high-fidelity simulation in advanced life support training: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Zeng Qin, Wang Kai, Liu Wei-xin, Zeng Jiu-zhi, Li Xing-lan, Zhang Qing-feng, Ren Shang-qing, Xu Wen-ming. (2023). Efficacy of high-fidelity simulation in advanced life support training: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04654-x
title: Achieve high efficacy of HF simulation-based ALS training through proper participants, well-designed courses, experienced instructors, and debriefing sessions
description: The article argues that HF simulation is "just a device that provides realistic feedback" and that high-efficacy ALS training additionally requires optimized course design, case scenarios, experienced instructors, and debriefing sessions. It links this to its moderator findings: benefits appeared for residents and senior students but not first-year students. Debriefing is described as providing feedback crucial to enhancing team performance.
requirements: High-efficacy ALS training needs optimized course design, case scenarios, experienced instructors, and debriefing sessions, per the article's discussion.
constraints: HF simulation is costly and time-consuming, requiring specialized personnel, equipment, and space; a cited cost-effectiveness analysis found HF programs had only a 6% probability of being cost-effective at a willingness to pay of $100 compared with LF programs.
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 25 RCTs in which 998 trainees used HF manikins (SimMan 3G by Laerdal was the most widely used simulator) and 989 received LF simulation-based or traditional training.
key_sources: Zeng Qin, Wang Kai, Liu Wei-xin, Zeng Jiu-zhi, Li Xing-lan, Zhang Qing-feng, Ren Shang-qing, Xu Wen-ming. (2023). Efficacy of high-fidelity simulation in advanced life support training: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04654-x

article_title: The Impact of High-Fidelity Simulation and Curriculum Integration on Nursing Students' Competence and Satisfaction: A Quasiexperimental Study.
citation: Ismail Ahmad, Al-Modallal Hanan, Aldardeir Njoud, Gomma Nada, Eltohamy Nadia Abd ElHamed. (2026). The Impact of High‐Fidelity Simulation and Curriculum Integration on Nursing Students’ Competence and Satisfaction: A Quasiexperimental Study. Journal of Nursing Management. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13140285/
title: HFS/curriculum-integrated session pattern: horizontally integrated scenario-based simulation with hands-on practice and debriefing in small groups
description: This pattern combines a horizontally integrated curriculum (merging disciplines within one time frame, here third-year women's health and child health nursing) with high-fidelity simulation using computerized manikins. Students practice paired maternal/newborn scenarios in small groups, followed by structured debriefing. The article's protocol comprised "HFS using birthing manikins, hands-on practice, scenario-based learning" for delivery management, newborn care with newborn manikins, and a 30-minute debriefing to "promote reflection, and improve clinical performance."
requirements: Students must already have been exposed to the topics separately in each course before the integrated session
Instructors adequately trained in the equipment and HFS manikins
A prepared protocol covering both the vaginal delivery and newborn care parts
constraints: Assessed only for two topics (vaginal delivery management and immediate newborn care) in one institution
Small convenient sample; findings may not generalize to other nursing programs or contexts
target_learning_goals: nursing management during normal vaginal delivery
examples: Five three-hour sessions with six students per session were conducted in the simulation laboratory in December 2023, with data collected two weeks after the intervention
key_sources: Ismail Ahmad, Al-Modallal Hanan, Aldardeir Njoud, Gomma Nada, Eltohamy Nadia Abd ElHamed. (2026). The Impact of High‐Fidelity Simulation and Curriculum Integration on Nursing Students’ Competence and Satisfaction: A Quasiexperimental Study. Journal of Nursing Management. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13140285/

article_title: The effect of high-fidelity simulation on nursing students' self-confidence and stress levels during patient intervention: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Yurt Seher, Açıkgoz Gizem, Aksoy Zahide, Akgun Feride Saruhan, Demirel Ayşen, Karaca Özge, Okuroğlu Gülten. (2026). The effect of high-fidelity simulation on nursing students’ self-confidence and stress levels during patient intervention: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education, 26, 477. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08828-1
title: High-fidelity hypovolemic shock simulation scenario with PEARLS pre-briefing and debriefing
description: A 10-minute simulated hypovolemic shock scenario in a replicated single-patient ICU room, developed using Healthcare Simulation Best Practice Standards, piloted with five third-year nursing students, and reviewed by two simulation experts. The plan specified pre-briefing (10 minutes), scenario (10 minutes) and debriefing (30 minutes), with "Method: PEARLS" debriefing and four scenario objectives including communication, teamwork, patient assessment and hypovolemic shock interventions. Sessions included 4–5 students, each participating once.
requirements: Developed using Healthcare Simulation Best Practice Standards and reviewed by two simulation experts
Piloted prior to the main study for clarity, feasibility, and realism
constraints: Scheduling prevented interactions between students who had and had not yet completed the simulation
examples: The 42-year-old ICU patient scenario with mitral valve insufficiency, delivered three days after a three-session theoretical lecture on shock
key_sources: Yurt Seher, Açıkgoz Gizem, Aksoy Zahide, Akgun Feride Saruhan, Demirel Ayşen, Karaca Özge, Okuroğlu Gülten. (2026). The effect of high-fidelity simulation on nursing students’ self-confidence and stress levels during patient intervention: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education, 26, 477. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08828-1

article_title: High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for training undergraduate medical students in pediatric emergencies: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Moliterno Nathalia Veiga, Paravidino Vitor Barreto, Robaina Jaqueline Rodrigues, Lima-Setta Fernanda, da Cunha Antônio José Ledo Alves, Prata-Barbosa Arnaldo, de Magalhães-Barbosa Maria Clara. (2024). High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for training undergraduate medical students in pediatric emergencies: a quasi-experimental study. Jornal de Pediatria. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jped.2024.03.007
title: High-fidelity simulation session pattern: scenario simulation followed by structured 40-minute debriefing with rotating active-player roles
description: This pattern organizes each simulation session around a case presentation, a 15–20 minute simulated emergency with a high-fidelity mannequin, and a debriefing in which "The students' performances were discussed with teachers, pointing out adequate and inadequate actions and procedures". Five to ten students participate per scenario, with two as active players and the rest as observers, and "The students' roles changed with each scenario so that all students had the opportunity to be active players or observers". Three teachers run each session: two role-play parents and health team members, one commands the simulator responses. Each student completed seven one-hour topic sessions (7 h total).
requirements: A high-fidelity full-body computerized patient simulator (PediaSIM in this study) programmed to provide realistic physiological responses
Multiple teachers to role-play parents and team members and to operate the simulator
A debriefing period with teachers discussing adequate and inadequate actions
constraints: The study used five to ten students per scenario with only two active players at a time, others observing
target_learning_goals: Pediatric emergency management: clinical reasoning, communication, attitude, leadership
examples: Seven pediatric emergency topics (wheezing infants, hypovolemic shock, pneumonia/septic shock, anaphylaxis, neonatal hypoglycemia, seizures, organophosphate poisoning) each taught in an approximately one-hour session with a 40-minute debriefing
key_sources: Moliterno Nathalia Veiga, Paravidino Vitor Barreto, Robaina Jaqueline Rodrigues, Lima-Setta Fernanda, da Cunha Antônio José Ledo Alves, Prata-Barbosa Arnaldo, de Magalhães-Barbosa Maria Clara. (2024). High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for training undergraduate medical students in pediatric emergencies: a quasi-experimental study. Jornal de Pediatria. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jped.2024.03.007

article_title: High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for training undergraduate medical students in pediatric emergencies: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Moliterno Nathalia Veiga, Paravidino Vitor Barreto, Robaina Jaqueline Rodrigues, Lima-Setta Fernanda, da Cunha Antônio José Ledo Alves, Prata-Barbosa Arnaldo, de Magalhães-Barbosa Maria Clara. (2024). High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for training undergraduate medical students in pediatric emergencies: a quasi-experimental study. Jornal de Pediatria. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jped.2024.03.007
title: Use high-fidelity simulation to develop technical and non-technical skills (clinical reasoning, communication, attitude, leadership) in undergraduate pediatric emergency training
description: The article argues simulation is especially valuable in pediatrics because severe acute events occur infrequently, so students get little real exposure; simulation fills this gap for technical skills, resuscitation, crisis management, and teamwork. Its results "support the need for training technical and non-technical skills related to behavior, attitude, leadership, and communication during undergraduate degrees", and the authors report the positive impact "resulted in the expansion and earlier introduction of the method in the curriculum", now inserted since the pre-internship in pediatrics.
requirements: A simulation laboratory with high-fidelity pediatric patient simulators
Trained faculty to run scenarios and debriefings
Standardized scenario checklists with content validity for assessment
constraints: The study was conducted in a single educational institution with a specific physical structure and human resources, limiting generalization to other institutions
Non-randomized allocation by schedule convenience and a pandemic-reduced sample size
target_learning_goals: Pediatric emergency care competencies: clinical reasoning, communication, attitude, leadership
examples: The study institution expanded HFS in the pediatric curriculum and introduced it earlier, from the pre-internship, after the study
key_sources: Moliterno Nathalia Veiga, Paravidino Vitor Barreto, Robaina Jaqueline Rodrigues, Lima-Setta Fernanda, da Cunha Antônio José Ledo Alves, Prata-Barbosa Arnaldo, de Magalhães-Barbosa Maria Clara. (2024). High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for training undergraduate medical students in pediatric emergencies: a quasi-experimental study. Jornal de Pediatria. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jped.2024.03.007

article_title: Comparison of simulation and video-based training for acute asthma.
citation: Grissa Mohamed Habib et al. (2023). Comparison of simulation and video-based training for acute asthma. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04836-7
title: Use high-fidelity simulation rather than interactive video-case training to teach management of high-risk emergency conditions such as acute asthma
description: The article supports high-fidelity simulation-based training — briefing, scenario, and debriefing on a full-scale patient simulator with real-time physiologically accurate feedback — over interactive video-case challenge for teaching acute asthma management. It reports that HFS "led to more long-term knowledge retention in the management of simulated acute asthma patients" and produced higher clinical and teamwork scores. The recommendation applies to final-year medical students in emergency medicine attachments.
requirements: Access to a full-scale patient simulator and trained instructors; the study used two instructors per simulation session and sessions of approximately 1 hour with equivalent key concepts across methods.
constraints: Evidence is from a single randomized study with a relatively low sample size; the IVC comparator is not a usual reference teaching method; transfer to daily clinical practice and impact on patient outcomes remain untested.
target_learning_goals: management of acute asthma exacerbation in the emergency department, including severity assessment and therapeutic management
examples: 69 final-year medical students were randomized to HFS (n = 34) or IVC (n = 35); the HFS group participated in a simulation session with an acute asthma scenario including briefing, scenario, and debriefing on a Laerdal SimMan 3G full-scale patient simulator.
key_sources: Grissa Mohamed Habib et al. (2023). Comparison of simulation and video-based training for acute asthma. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04836-7
